title: Design Search Autocomplete System
description: Brute force to optimized: a flat map rescanned on every keystroke versus a Trie caching sentence counts at every node along each insertion path.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a search autocomplete system, initialized with historical sentences and their hot degrees (how many times each was searched). Implement input(c): if c is a lowercase letter or space, append it to the currently typed sentence and return the top 3 historical sentences that start with the currently typed prefix, sorted by hot degree descending (ties broken lexicographically ascending); if c is "#", the current sentence is finished, its hot degree is incremented by 1 (or it is added as new with degree 1), the typed sentence resets, and an empty list is returned.

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Prefix-based lookup across many stored strings, queried incrementally character by character\"","A Trie, the standard structure for prefix-based string queries"],["\"Top-k matches by a score, at every prefix\"","Cache each Trie node with the counts of every complete sentence passing through it, avoiding a full rescan per keystroke"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

As the user types character by character, each new character narrows the "currently typed prefix," and the system must instantly report the top 3 known sentences matching that (growing) prefix. Since typing happens one character at a time, the system should ideally NOT need to re-examine every historical sentence on every single keystroke.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Search Box Suggesting Popular Past Searches
blocks.text: Picture typing into a search box, and after every letter, the box instantly suggests the 3 most popular past searches starting with what you have typed so far. As you type each new letter, only searches matching so far need re-considering, not the entire search history from scratch.

blocks.caption: A Trie over historical sentences, with each node caching the counts of sentences passing through it

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: sentences = ["i love you","island","iroman","i love leetcode"], times = [5,3,2,2]

blocks.content: {"headers":["input(c)","Result"],"rows":[["input('i')","[\"i love you\",\"island\",\"i love leetcode\"]"],["input(' ')","[\"i love you\",\"i love leetcode\"]"],["input('a')","[] (no sentence starts with \"i a\")"],["input('#')","[] (finishes and records \"i a\" as a new sentence with degree 1)"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before scanning every historical sentence on every single keystroke to check for a prefix match, notice that a Trie naturally represents shared prefixes as shared paths, and if each Trie node CACHES the counts of every complete sentence passing through it, each keystroke only needs to walk one more character down the Trie and read off that node's cached top matches directly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A Trie organizes strings so that all strings sharing a prefix share the same path down to that prefix's node, making "which sentences start with X" naturally correspond to "everything reachable from X's Trie node."

Observation 2: If every Trie node stores a small map of {complete sentence: hot degree} for every sentence that PASSES THROUGH it (not just ends there), then finding the top 3 matches for any prefix is just reading that node's stored map directly, no traversal needed at query time.

Observation 3: Since input() is called one character at a time, maintaining a "current Trie node" pointer that advances by exactly one child link per call means each keystroke does O(1) work to move, plus O(entries at that node log entries) to sort and pick the top 3.

Observation 4: On "#", the currently typed sentence is inserted (or its count incremented) into the Trie along its entire path, updating every node's cached map along the way, and the "current node" pointer resets to the Trie root for the next sentence.

This leads to a Trie where each node caches {sentence: count} for every sentence passing through it, maintaining a "current node" pointer that advances one step per input(c) call, reading off the top 3 from that node's cache directly.
6. Brute Force Solution
Maintain a flat map from sentence to its hot degree. On every input(c) call, scan ALL sentences in this map to find those starting with the currently typed prefix, sort matches, and return the top 3.
Step by step algorithm

items: Maintain a flat hash map from sentence to hot degree, initialized from the constructor arguments.
On input(c) with c not "#", append c to the current typed string; scan the ENTIRE map for sentences starting with this prefix.
Sort matches by degree descending, then lexicographically; return the top 3.
On input('#'), increment (or insert) the current sentence's count in the map, reset the typed string, and return [].

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A flat map plus a full scan per keystroke directly implements the definition, correctly checking every sentence's prefix match.
Rescanning ALL sentences on EVERY keystroke wastes work, especially as the historical sentence collection grows large.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(total sentences times average sentence length) per input(c) call, for the full scan and comparison.
Space: O(total sentences times average length).

Limitation: a Trie, with each node caching the sentences passing through it, lets each keystroke do O(1) traversal plus a sort over only the ALREADY-NARROWED candidates at that node, avoiding any full rescan.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why full rescanning is wasteful: as more characters are typed, the set of matching sentences only ever SHRINKS (or stays the same), never grows, so re-checking sentences that already stopped matching is unnecessary repeated work.

The Trie-with-cached-counts design: build a Trie over all historical sentences; at EVERY node along a sentence's path (not just its terminal node), record that sentence's current hot degree in that node's local map.

Why this speeds up queries: the "current Trie node" pointer, maintained across successive input(c) calls, always represents exactly the currently typed prefix's node; its cached map already contains precisely the sentences matching that prefix, with no need to filter anything else.

The core idea: cache prefix-matching sentences directly at each Trie node during insertion, so each keystroke's query becomes reading and sorting only the relevant node's small cached map.

Build a Trie where every node caches {sentence: count} for every sentence passing through it (updated at insertion time along the whole path). Maintain a current-node pointer, advancing by one child link per input(c) call (or null if no branch exists); read the top 3 from the current node's cache. On "#", insert (or increment) the finished sentence along its full path and reset to the root.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for sentences=["i love you","island","iroman","i love leetcode"], times=[5,3,2,2]

blocks.content: {"headers":["input(c)","Trie node reached","Cached sentences at that node","Result"],"rows":[["'i'","node for prefix \"i\"","{i love you:5, island:3, iroman:2, i love leetcode:2}","[\"i love you\",\"island\",\"i love leetcode\"]"],["' '","node for prefix \"i \"","{i love you:5, i love leetcode:2}","[\"i love you\",\"i love leetcode\"]"],["'a'","no child \"a\" exists at \"i a\" node -> null","none","[]"]]}

blocks.caption: Each keystroke advances the current Trie node by one; its cached map is read and sorted directly

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since every sentence is inserted along its ENTIRE Trie path (not just at its terminal node), each node's cached map exactly reflects every historical sentence sharing that node's prefix, along with its up-to-date hot degree. Maintaining a "current node" pointer that advances one child link per keystroke means each input(c) call does only O(1) traversal work, plus sorting the (typically small) set of already-matching candidates cached at that specific node, correctly reproducing the same result as a full rescan but without ever re-examining non-matching sentences.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(sentence length) total for insertion (spread across "#" calls), O(m log m) per input(c) call, m being the number of sentences sharing the current prefix (typically small).
Space: O(total characters across all sentences times average matching count per node) for the Trie and its cached maps.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Design Search Autocomplete System is the canonical Trie-based prefix-query design problem, showing how caching relevant data directly AT each Trie node avoids full rescans on every incremental query.
Common Mistakes

items: Only recording a sentence at its FINAL Trie node instead of at every node along its path, breaking the ability to answer prefix queries directly from intermediate nodes.
Forgetting to handle the "current node became null" case (no sentence shares this prefix), which must persist as null until the next "#" resets it.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Typing a prefix that matches no historical sentence at all","Returns [] for that and all subsequent characters until the next \"#\"."],["Finishing a brand new sentence never seen before","It is added with hot degree 1, becoming a candidate for future queries."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "cache the relevant sentences AT each Trie node during insertion, not just search on demand" is the key insight that turns a rescan-per-keystroke design into an efficient one.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "prefix-based lookup queried incrementally, one character at a time", think: a Trie with cached results at each node, and a pointer that advances one step per query.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you bound memory if the historical sentence collection grows very large (e.g., evicting rarely used cached entries)?
How would you support deleting a historical sentence from the system?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree), the foundational structure this problem builds upon.
Any "incremental prefix query, top-k by score" design problem, solvable via a Trie with per-node cached rankings.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The flat-map rescan approach costs O(total sentences times length) per keystroke; the Trie-with-cached-counts approach costs O(m log m) per keystroke, m being only the sentences actually sharing the current prefix, the standard efficient design.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a Trie caching relevant sentence data at every node along each sentence's path, enabling O(1) traversal per keystroke.
Core Idea: maintain a current-node pointer advancing one character per input(c) call; read and sort that node's cached {sentence: count} map for the top 3.
Time: O(total sentences times length) per call for the flat-map rescan, O(m log m) per call for the Trie approach.
Space: O(total sentences times length) versus O(total chars times average matches per node).
Most Important Observation: caching matching sentences directly at each Trie node during insertion avoids ever rescanning non-matching sentences at query time.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, moderately hard Trie-based design problem, foundational to real autocomplete systems.
One line memory trick: a Trie caching sentence counts at every node; advance one node per keystroke, read its cache.
